coaching.coaching: Run a quick pre-mortem on signal windows during the delete call: how could this plan fail?
coaching.subject: signal windows during the delete call

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)

evidence: 2 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add ACs for: the interrupt notice (exit 143, 'interrupted'/'may not hold', no 'SSM was NOT'); no 'already replaced' on success or on a failure after the SSM write; no notice when both the delete and the generator fail.
evidence: AC2: 'A test drives the generator-failure and SSM-failure paths'
Testing lists an 'Interrupt test', 'No false claim, delete failed', 'No false claim after the write', and the happy-path edit, none of which any AC names
Approach: 'Disarmed with `trap - EXIT HUP INT TERM` immediately after `aws ssm put-parameter` succeeds'
findings.finding: Several behaviours the plan delivers have no covering acceptance criterion. These are: the interrupt notice (exit 129/130/143 with 'may not hold'), the disarm guarantee (no false notice after a successful SSM write), arming after the generator when the delete failed, and absence of the notice on the happy path. The ACs cover only the generator-failure and SSM-failure paths.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria (AC1, AC2) vs Approach / Testing
scenarios: A regression in the disarm placement (notice printed after a successful rotation) satisfies both ACs as written.
The interrupt handlers could be dropped and the ACs would still be checked.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC: 'An interrupt test and the no-false-claim tests (delete+generator fail; mktemp fails after the SSM write; happy path) pass, asserting the interrupt notice / absence of the lockout notice as described in Testing.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the mktemp stub fail only on `mktemp -d`, and assert that the recorded argv contains `ssm put-parameter` (and `--generate-http-password`) before asserting no 'already replaced'.
evidence: 'SSM succeeds, then the `mktemp` stub exits 1 before step 5 installs its own trap: asserts a non-zero exit and no "already replaced"'
There is no assertion that `aws ssm put-parameter` was recorded, or that the failure came from `mktemp -d`.
findings.finding: The 'No false claim after the write' test asserts only a non-zero exit and the absence of 'already replaced'. The mktemp stub 'can fail', but the plan does not say it fails only on `mktemp -d` or that the test confirms the SSM write happened. If the script calls mktemp earlier, or a stub misconfiguration fails some earlier step, the test passes without ever reaching the post-write window it is meant to guard.
findings.location: Testing — 'No false claim after the write'; Scope — 'add a `mktemp` stub that can fail'
scenarios: mktemp is used before the delete (e.g. for a temp file), so the stub fails there: exit is non-zero, no notice is printed, and the test passes vacuously.
A future refactor moves the disarm after `mktemp -d`; the test still passes only if the stub happened to fail earlier.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the mktemp stub exit 1 only when its argv contains `-d`, otherwise exec the real mktemp. In the test, assert the argv log contains the put-parameter call and the stub's `-d` invocation, then assert a non-zero exit and the notice's absence.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm the substrings the existing shape-check tests assert, and either keep them verbatim in rotation_notice's failure message or list the shape-check test edits in Scope.
evidence: Context: 'Gerrit's token was already replaced, SSM was not updated, and the review-bot cannot authenticate until a re-run succeeds'
Approach: '... SSM was NOT updated; the review-bot cannot authenticate until this script succeeds'
findings.finding: The plan says the existing shape-check tests 'keep passing unchanged', but the branch's notice text is being replaced. The existing tests assert the old wording from 35c1983cb07. The Context paraphrases that notice as 'SSM was not updated' and 'until a re-run succeeds'. The new rotation_notice says 'SSM was NOT updated' and 'until this script succeeds'. If the existing assertions are case-sensitive, or match 're-run', they will fail. The plan neither shows the asserted substrings nor commits to keeping them.
findings.location: Testing — 'The existing shape-check tests keep passing unchanged'; Approach — rotation_notice wording; Scope — 'remove the duplicated notice lines from the shape-check branch'
scenarios: An existing test asserts 'SSM was not updated' or 're-run' and breaks after the shape-check branch delegates to the trap.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Amend AC1 to carve out interrupts (hedged 'may not hold' wording, exit 128+signal), and add an AC requiring no notice when nothing was replaced or after a successful SSM write, each backed by the planned tests.
evidence: AC1: "When `service-user.sh` fails at any step after deleting the bot's `default` token ... it tells the operator on stderr that Gerrit's token was replaced, SSM was not updated, and the review-bot cannot authenticate"
Approach: for an interrupt it "says ... that SSM may not hold the new token, and that the review-bot may be unable to authenticate"
Testing: "Asserts exit 143, the \"interrupted\" / \"may not hold\" notice, and that \"SSM was NOT\" is absent."
AC2 covers only "the generator-failure and SSM-failure paths".
findings.finding: The Acceptance Criteria omit two behaviors the plan deliberately builds and tests. The first is the interrupt notice semantics: the hedged 'may not hold' wording and exits 129/130/143. The second is the no-false-claim guarantees: no notice when the delete and generator both fail, and none after a successful SSM write. AC1 also says that on failure 'at any step' the script states 'SSM was not updated' and that the bot 'cannot authenticate'. This contradicts the Approach's interrupt notice, which must not claim SSM was not updated, and the interrupt test, which asserts 'SSM was NOT' is absent.
scenarios: An implementer satisfies AC1 literally by printing 'SSM was NOT updated' on interrupts too. The planned interrupt test then fails, or the implementer drops the hedge and misleads operators after a write that actually committed.
A late or missing `trap -` regresses into a false 'already replaced' claim after a successful write, and no AC requires that case to be checked.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: "- [ ] On HUP/INT/TERM after the token is replaced, the script exits 129/130/143 and says SSM may not hold the new token, never that it was NOT updated." and "- [ ] No 'already replaced' notice is printed when both delete and generator fail, or when a failure occurs after the SSM write succeeds (tested via the delete-failure and mktemp-failure cases)."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reword AC1 to cover non-signal failures only, and add the interrupt case with its hedged 'may not hold' wording.
evidence: AC1: 'tells the operator on stderr that Gerrit's token was replaced, SSM was not updated, and the review-bot cannot authenticate'
Approach: 'For an interrupt ... says ... that SSM may not hold the new token'
Testing: 'Asserts exit 143, the "interrupted" / "may not hold" notice, and that "SSM was NOT" is absent.'
findings.finding: AC1 requires the notice for any failure after the delete and before the SSM write succeeds to say that SSM 'was not updated' and that the bot 'cannot authenticate'. The Approach deliberately prints a different, hedged message ('may not hold', 'may be unable') when that window is ended by a signal. The interrupt test even asserts 'SSM was NOT' is absent. AC1 does not carve out interrupts, so the two sections point the implementer in different directions.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria AC1 vs Approach (rotation_notice interrupt branch) / Testing (Interrupt test)
scenarios: An implementer who satisfies AC1 literally prints 'SSM was NOT updated' on SIGTERM and fails the interrupt test.
A verifier judging AC1 marks the interrupt path non-compliant.
findings.suggested_fix: AC1: 'When service-user.sh exits non-zero (not by signal) after Gerrit's token may have been replaced and before the SSM write succeeds, it prints ... ; when interrupted by HUP/INT/TERM in that window it prints that SSM may not hold the new token ...'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that `interrupted=0` is initialized before the first `arm_lockout_notice`, or that `rotation_notice` reads `${interrupted:-0}`, so the EXIT trap is safe under `set -u`.
evidence: "HUP/INT/TERM traps that set a shell variable `interrupted=1`"
Context: "`set -euo pipefail` exits silently on them"
No initialization of `interrupted` is specified anywhere in Approach or Scope.
findings.finding: `rotation_notice` branches on `interrupted`, which the plan says only the HUP/INT/TERM handlers set. The script runs under `set -euo pipefail`. On the plain failure path, which is the main case, `interrupted` is unbound. Expanding `$interrupted` inside the EXIT trap then aborts with 'unbound variable', so the notice may never print. The plan never says to initialize the variable.
scenarios: The generator exits 1 after the delete. The EXIT trap runs `rotation_notice`, which references the unset `$interrupted`. bash reports an unbound variable and the 'already replaced' notice is not printed. This is exactly the silent lockout the plan exists to remove.
findings.suggested_fix: Set `interrupted=0` at script top (or inside `arm_lockout_notice` before installing traps), and have `rotation_notice` test `"${interrupted:-0}" = 1`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say that `interrupted=0` is set before any trap is armed (for example inside `arm_lockout_notice`, or at the top of step 3), or that `rotation_notice` reads it as `${interrupted:-0}`, so the EXIT trap is safe under `set -u`.
evidence: infra/gerrit/service-user.sh:11 `set -euo pipefail`
Plan: 'HUP/INT/TERM traps that set a shell variable `interrupted=1` and `exit 129/130/143`'
The plan names no initialization (`interrupted=0`) and no defaulted expansion (`${interrupted:-0}`)
findings.finding: The plan says the signal handlers 'set a shell variable `interrupted=1`' and that `rotation_notice` uses it to tell an interrupt from a failure. It never says where `interrupted` gets its starting value. The script runs under `set -u`, so in the failure case (no signal arrived) a bare `$interrupted` in `rotation_notice` is unbound. bash then reports 'unbound variable' inside the EXIT trap and aborts the trap, so the lockout notice this plan exists to add would never print.
scenarios: The generator exits 1 after a successful delete: `set -e` exits, the EXIT trap runs `rotation_notice`, the test of `$interrupted` hits an unbound variable, and the operator sees 'interrupted: unbound variable' instead of the lockout notice.
The SSM write fails with exit 254: same outcome.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach, add: '`arm_lockout_notice` initializes `interrupted=${interrupted:-0}` before installing traps, and `rotation_notice` tests `[ "${interrupted:-0}" = 1 ]`, so the trap is safe under `set -u`.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Install the HUP/INT/TERM handlers (with the hedged 'interrupted, may not hold' wording) before the delete is issued, or document why a signal during the in-flight delete or generator is out of scope.
evidence: "Fix the class rather than add more per-step branches: an `EXIT` trap prints a notice ... whenever the script exits while Gerrit may hold a token SSM does not."
Root cause: "every other way out between the delete and the SSM write is an implicit `set -e` exit or a signal"
Arming points are only after the delete returns success and after the generator returns success.
findings.finding: The plan claims to 'fix the class' of silent lockouts, but leaves signal windows unarmed. The first window is a SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP while `gerrit set-account --delete-token default` is in flight. The server may already have committed the delete, yet arming only happens after the delete returns success. The second window is a signal while `--generate-http-password` runs after a failed delete. The server may already have generated the token, yet the re-arm only happens after the generator returns. In both cases the script dies by signal with no notice while Gerrit may no longer match SSM.
findings.location: Approach — "Armed when `gerrit set-account --delete-token default` succeeds" / "Armed (again, idempotently) right after `--generate-http-password` succeeds"
scenarios: The operator presses Ctrl-C while the delete's ssh is running. The delete committed server-side, the bot's token is gone and SSM is stale, and the script exits 130 with no notice.
The delete returned 255 (transient), then SIGTERM arrives while the generator is running and the server has already issued a new token. No trap is armed, so there is no notice.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Cover the delete's in-flight window: install the HUP/INT/TERM handlers, with the hedged 'interrupted… may' wording, before issuing the delete, or explicitly state and justify why an interrupt or ambiguous ssh failure during the delete is out of scope.
evidence: Plan: 'A failed delete (Gerrit unreachable, or no `default` token yet) has replaced nothing, so it arms nothing'
Plan: HUP/INT/TERM handlers are installed only by `arm_lockout_notice`, which first runs after the delete succeeds
infra/gerrit/service-user.sh:57: the delete is a remote ssh command whose server-side effect can commit even when ssh exits non-zero
findings.finding: Nothing is armed until the delete reports success, so the delete call itself is uncovered. If the operator presses Ctrl-C (or sends TERM/HUP) while `gerrit set-account --delete-token default` is in flight, the default signal action kills the script. Gerrit may already have deleted the token, and the operator gets no notice. The same applies when ssh exits 255 because the connection dropped after the server committed the delete: the plan treats that as 'has replaced nothing'. If the generator then also fails (for example the network is still down), the bot has no valid token, and the 'delete and generator both fail → no already replaced' test locks in the silence. The plan's claim that 'every other way out between the delete and the SSM write' is covered therefore leaves out the delete's own in-flight window.
findings.location: Approach — 'Armed when `gerrit set-account --delete-token default` succeeds' bullet; Testing — 'No false claim, delete failed'
scenarios: The operator presses Ctrl-C during a slow delete ssh. Gerrit has already removed the default token. The script dies with no notice and the review-bot is locked out.
ssh exits 255 on a transport drop after the delete committed, and the generator fails on the same outage. The script exits 255 silently and the bot is locked out.
